power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objective: Motivational incongruence refers to insufficient satisfaction of individual motives in interaction with the environment and is assumed to contribute to psychological distress and psychopathology when prolonged.

This study examined reduced motivational incongruence as a potential change mechanism in psychotherapy by testing whether within-person decreases in motivational incongruence predict subsequent decreases in general psychological distress.
Method: Analyses were based on three psychotherapy samples from two randomized controlled trials and one observational dataset collected in routine care, comprising 1,656 patients in total.

In each sample, motivational incongruence and distress were assessed at four to six occasions during treatment using short forms of the Incongruence Questionnaire and the Symptom Checklist-90-R, respectively.
Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs) tested prospective within-person effects between motivational incongruence and distress.
Latent curve models with structured residuals (LCM-SRs) served as exploratory robustness analyses.
Results: Across three samples, the RI-CLPMs yielded significant and large prospective effects of motivational incongruence on subsequent distress.
Reverse cross-lagged effects, from distress to subsequent motivational incongruence, were significant in two of the three samples.
The exploratory LCM-SR supported the primary motivational incongruence-to-distress effect in one sample but yielded no admissible solutions in the other two.

Conclusions: Across three independent psychotherapy samples, within-person reductions in motivational incongruence preceded reductions in distress, consistent with motivational incongruence as a potential transtheoretical change mechanism in psychotherapy.
Motivational incongruence may therefore represent a candidate treatment target.

Future research should test the proposed causal MOTIVATIONAL INCONGRUENCE AS A CHANGE MECHANISM 3 relationship experimentally and examine which dimensions of motivational incongruence are most relevant for individual patients.
Understanding how patients improve in psychotherapy requires identifying the mechanisms through which change occurs.
Importantly, evidence for a potential mechanism needs more than showing that a proposed process is associated with the outcome or changes during treatment (Cuijpers et al., 2019; Kazdin, 2007).

text.text: Specifically, a proposed mechanism should precede the outcome it is assumed to influence and not just be associated with unclear temporal direction (Kazdin, 2009).

text.text: Change processes are therapist activities and patient responses occurring within sessions, whereas change mechanisms are patient-level developments in characteristics or skills that are hypothesized to contribute to improvement but cannot be controlled directly by the therapist.

text.text: Reduced motivational incongruence might represent such a transtheoretical patient-level change mechanism.

According to consistency theory, human mental functioning is oriented toward satisfying basic psychological needs, which individuals pursue through approach and avoidance motives and the behaviors that serve them (Grawe, 2007).

text.text: Approach motives represent desired interactions with the environment or oneself that may satisfy psychological needs, whereas avoidance motives represent experiences or outcomes that individuals seek to prevent because they may threaten these needs (Grosse Holtforth & Grawe, 2003).

text.text: Accordingly, a decrease in motivational incongruence (i.e., better motive satisfaction) may represent a transtheoretical change mechanism through which psychological distress may decrease during psychotherapy.
Conversely, psychological disorders may themselves impede motive satisfaction, suggesting a reciprocal relationship between motivational incongruence and distress (Grosse Holtforth & Grawe, 2003).

text.text: Several findings support the relevance of motivational incongruence for psychological distress: Cross-sectional findings indicate that psychotherapy patients report higher motivational incongruence than nonclinical participants (Grosse Holtforth & Grawe, 2003; Lutz et al., 2006), and that motivational incongruence is substantially associated with greater psychological distress and depressive symptom severity, as well as lower subjective well-being (Grosse Holtforth & Grawe, 2003).

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that motivational incongruence is elevated in clinical samples, decreases during treatment, and covaries with psychological distress.

None of these designs, however, can establish whether changes in motivational incongruence precede changes in distress, which is a necessary condition for a change mechanism (Crits-Christoph & Gibbons, 2021; Kazdin, 2007).

text.text: For motivational incongruence, such tests are lacking in psychotherapy samples.

Accordingly, previous studies have called for research clarifying the direction of the relationship between incongruence and psychological distress (Berking et al., 2003; Scheidegger et al., 2023; Vincent et al., 2021).

text.text: The only cross-lagged study to date, conducted in a nonclinical sample with intervals of two to three years, found that better mental health consistently predicted lower subsequent motivational incongruence, whereas the reverse association emerged at only one interval and was weak and opposite to expectation (Bachmann et al., 2014).

text.text: However, this study did not distinguish stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations.
Three methodological considerations are central to examining these associations.

First, distinguishing between-person and within-person associations is essential to psychotherapy mechanism research (Falkenström et al., 2020), as illustrated by research on the therapeutic alliance (Zilcha-Mano, 2017).

text.text: Unlike the traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM), which can conflate these levels, the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) separates patients' stable, trait-like levels from occasion-specific deviations.

Correlations between the random intercepts indicate whether patients who are generally more incongruent are also generally more distressed, whereas cross-lagged paths indicate whether deviations in motivational incongruence predict subsequent deviations in distress, and vice versa (Falkenström, 2024; Hamaker et al., 2015).

text.text: This separation strengthens the validity of causal inference compared with analyses that conflate within-person and between-person associations (Falkenström, 2024; Falkenström et al., 2020).

text.text: Second, systematic change during psychotherapy can introduce time trends.
Unmodeled trends in either construct, including correlated individual differences in change, can bias autoregressive and cross-lagged estimates under certain conditions (Falkenström et al., 2026).

text.text: Accounting for these trends therefore reduces the risk of biased findings.
A third consideration is reverse causality, in which the presumed outcome causes the presumed predictor.

The RI-CLPM examines both directions within a single model: the effect of motivational incongruence on subsequent distress and the effect of distress on subsequent motivational incongruence are estimated simultaneously.
Both effects may operate simultaneously, as anticipated by consistency theory (Grosse Holtforth & Grawe, 2003; Scheidegger et al., 2023; Vincent et al., 2021).

text.text: The present study addressed the lack of prospective evidence on the relationship between motivational incongruence and general psychological distress during psychotherapy by examining reductions in motivational incongruence as a potential transtheoretical mechanism of change.

To this end, we tested the cross-lagged effects between motivational incongruence and general psychological distress using data from two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and one large routine-care sample, accounting for the three methodological considerations outlined above.
Evidence that reduced motivational incongruence predicts lower subsequent distress would support motivational incongruence as a candidate treatment target.
It would also provide a basis for future research on selecting which motive dimensions to address in treatment based on each patient's individual pattern of motivational incongruence.

We hypothesized that (a) within patients, lower motivational incongruence at one assessment predicts lower psychological distress at the next assessment, and (b) patients who generally report higher motivational incongruence than other patients also report higher psychological distress.

Because consistency theory also assumes that psychological disorders may interfere with motive satisfaction, we hypothesized that (c) within patients, lower psychological distress at one assessment predicts lower motivational incongruence at the next assessment.

The present study included data from two randomized controlled trials and one large routine-care sample to examine the temporal dynamics between motivational incongruence and general psychological distress across controlled and routine-care settings.

The statistical analyses were conducted in three steps.
First, in preliminary analyses, we tested for a trend in the data and determined the specific model used in the main analyses.

Second, in the main analyses, we used the resulting model (i.e., a detrended random-intercept cross-lagged panel model) to estimate prospective effects between motivational incongruence and general psychological distress.
Third, in exploratory analyses, we used an alternative approach to modeling the trend, namely, the latent curve model with structured residuals.
Because participants were assessed repeatedly while undergoing psychotherapy, the sample-level means of both constructs were expected to decline across waves as treatment progressed.

If left unmodeled, such temporal trends can bias autoregressive and cross-lagged estimates. Falkenström et al. (2026) showed that unmodeled time trends can bias these estimates under certain conditions.

text.text: Because such trends are to be expected in data collected during a clinical intervention, we addressed this issue in three steps.
First, we examined whether temporal mean trends were present in motivational incongruence and general psychological distress.
For each sample, we inspected the wave means visually.
We then compared a model in which the means of each construct were constrained to be equal across waves with a model in which they were estimated freely.

An RMSEAD above the cutoff of .08 was taken to indicate that the equalmeans model should not be retained and that mean trends should be modeled in the longitudinal analyses (for additional information on the tests of temporal mean trends, see the Supplemental Material, Part 3).
Second, following the procedure used by Falkenström et al. (2026), we examined whether temporal trends needed to be modeled within the RI-CLPMs.

text.text: For each sample, we compared two versions of the RI-CLPM: a nondetrended model in which the intercepts of observed variables were constrained to be equal across waves and a detrended model in which the intercepts of observed variables were estimated freely at each wave.
Model fit was compared using RMSEAD, with the more parsimonious model (i.e., the nondetrended model) retained only when RMSEAD was below the cutoff of .08.
Third, we tested whether the autoregressive and cross-lagged effects between motivational incongruence and distress were stable over time.

For each sample, we compared two versions of the RI-CLPM: one in which the autoregressive and cross-lagged effects were constrained to be equal across waves (Figure 1) and one in which these effects were estimated freely across waves.

text.text: As in the previous comparisons, RMSEAD was used to determine whether the more parsimonious constrained model could be retained.

To test for prospective effects between motivational incongruence and general psychological distress, we estimated detrended RI-CLPMs separately in the Bern and Zurich trial samples and in the Trier sample.
The models for the Bern and Zurich trial samples included four waves; the model for the Trier sample included six waves.
The RI-CLPM decomposed each observed score into a random intercept and a residualized wave-specific factor.
The random intercepts are time-invariant latent factors that capture stable between-person differences in motivational incongruence and psychological distress.
The random intercepts of the two constructs were allowed to correlate.
The residualized wave-specific factors capture occasionspecific within-person deviations from a person's expected level at each wave.
The autoregressive and cross-lagged effects were estimated among these residualized wave-specific factors.
The error terms of the residualized wave-specific factors were allowed to correlate within each wave.
In exploratory analyses, we used an alternative approach to modeling the trend.
Specifically, we estimated the same within-person dynamics using a latent curve model with structured residuals (LCM-SR; Curran et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Specifically, we estimated the same within-person dynamics using a latent curve model with structured residuals (LCM-SR; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Curran et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The LCM-SR builds on the RI-CLPM by adding a random linear slope factor for each construct; this slope factor captures between-person differences in the rate of change of motivational incongruence and distress over time.

Because the slope, autoregressive, and cross-lagged parameters were all estimated jointly in a single step, the resulting autoregressive and cross-lagged effects reflect the within-person reciprocal effects between motivational incongruence and distress after accounting for between-person differences in each construct's rate of change.
As in the main analyses, we compared a version of the LCM-SR in which the autoregressive and cross-lagged effects were constrained to be equal across waves with an unconstrained version.
Again, model fit was compared using RMSEAD to determine whether the more parsimonious constrained model could be retained.
We report the LCM-SR as an exploratory analysis because it is a demanding model that carries a relatively high risk that the estimation does not converge or does not converge properly.

text.text: The present study aimed to examine prospective within-person effects and betweenperson associations between motivational incongruence and general psychological distress in two randomized trials and one routine-care sample.

Our findings for the primary RI-CLPMs showed that at the within-person level, lower motivational incongruence at one assessment predicted lower general psychological distress at the subsequent assessment across all three samples.
Thus, the primary analyses supported the hypothesized (a) within-person association across controlled and routine-care psychotherapy contexts.
In contrast, the primary findings on the reverse cross-lagged within-person association, specified in hypothesis (c), were less consistent.
Lower psychological distress predicted lower subsequent motivational incongruence in the Zurich sample and Trier sample but not significantly in the Bern sample.
Thus, hypothesis (c) was supported in two of the three samples, providing evidence for a reciprocal prospective relationship in these samples.
At the between-person level, the random intercepts were positively associated across all samples, but significantly only in the Zurich sample and Trier sample.

This finding indicates that patients who reported generally higher motivational incongruence across treatment also reported MOTIVATIONAL INCONGRUENCE AS A CHANGE MECHANISM 22 higher distress across treatment.
Thus, hypothesis (b) was supported in two of three samples.

These between-person associations are consistent with previous cross-sectional findings showing substantial associations between motivational incongruence and general psychological distress (Grosse Holtforth & Grawe, 2003; Lutz et al., 2006; Scheidegger et al., 2023; Vincent et al., 2021).

text.text: Previous studies have shown that motivational incongruence is associated with psychological distress and decreases during psychotherapy (Berking et al., 2003; Grosse Holtforth & Grawe, 2003; Lutz et al., 2006; Scheidegger et al., 2023; Vincent et al., 2021).

text.text: The present findings extend this evidence by demonstrating temporal precedence and prospective within-person associations while separating stable between-person differences.
This strengthens the evidence for reduced motivational incongruence as a potential change mechanism.

The standardized prospective effects from motivational incongruence to distress were large in all three samples according to the empirical benchmarks proposed by Orth et al. (2024) for crosslagged effects.

text.text: The findings also extend the previous cross-lagged investigation of motivational incongruence and mental health (Bachmann et al., 2014).

text.text: In contrast to their findings, we found a consistent prospective motivational incongruence-to-distress association in psychotherapy samples, using substantially shorter assessment intervals and separating stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations.

This separation strengthens the case for potential causality, because observed or unobserved patient characteristics that remain stable over the study period cannot, by design, confound these within-person associations (Falkenström et al., 2020 (Falkenström et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: This separation strengthens the case for potential causality, because observed or unobserved patient characteristics that remain stable over the study period cannot, by design, confound these within-person associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Falkenström et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Falkenström et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the prospective associations observed in the present study cannot be explained by stable differences between patients that may be associated with both motivational incongruence and psychological distress.
An additional consideration concerns systematic change over treatment, as unmodeled longer-term trends could bias estimated cross-lagged effects (Falkenström et al., 2026).
text.formatted: An additional consideration concerns systematic change over treatment, as unmodeled longer-term trends could bias estimated cross-lagged effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Falkenström et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: To address this issue, the primary RI-CLPMs freely estimated occasion means to account for sample-level trends, while the exploratory LCM-SRs additionally accounted for between-person differences in linear rates of change.
The LCM-SRs yielded no admissible solutions in the Bern and Zurich samples.
Consequently, the robustness of the prospective associations after additionally accounting for individual treatment trajectories could not be examined in these samples.
In the Trier sample, the motivational incongruence-to-distress effect remained significant, whereas the reverse effect was small and not significant.

This provides additional support for the motivational incongruence-to-distress association, although the constrained model's near-boundary solution requires cautious interpretation and robustness could not be established across all three samples.

Despite these methodological strengths, the present analyses still do not establish causality, as the proposed mechanism was not experimentally manipulated and time-varying confounding remains possible.
Nevertheless, the findings are consistent with a mechanism interpretation and provide comparatively strong observational evidence for the proposed prospective relationship.

The prospective effects from psychological distress to motivational incongruence in the Zurich and Trier samples are consistent with consistency theory, which assumes that psychological disorders may themselves impair the satisfaction of an individual's motives (Grosse Holtforth & Grawe, 2003).

text.text: Importantly, such reciprocal effects do not contradict an understanding of reduced motivational incongruence as a potential change mechanism: a mechanism may contribute to subsequent symptom change while also being influenced by prior states of that outcome (Falkenström et al., 2022).

text.text: Notably, the prospective effects from motivational incongruence to distress (β = .13-.40) were numerically larger than the reverse effects (β = .02-.16) in each sample.

Because the bidirectional effects have the same sign, the pattern observed in the Zurich sample and Trier sample is consistent with a reinforcing feedback process, in which lower motivational incongruence may be followed by lower distress, which in turn may contribute to reduced motivational incongruence (Falkenström et al., 2022).

text.text: According to consistency theory, reduced motivational incongruence is assumed to be relevant across psychotherapeutic orientations.

Previous studies have shown that motivational incongruence decreases across different treatment settings and patient groups (Berking et al., 2003; Caspar et al., 2023; Lutz et al., 2006; Scheidegger et al., 2023; Vincent et al., 2021).

text.text: The present study extends this evidence by demonstrating consistent prospective within-person associations between motivational incongruence and subsequent psychological distress across two randomized trials and a routine-care sample that differed in treatment setting and patient population.
At the same time, all treatments shared a cognitive-behavioral foundation, although they differed in their therapeutic foci and integrated techniques from different therapeutic orientations.
Thus, the present study does not directly test generalizability across clearly distinct therapeutic orientations.
Replication across such orientations would provide a stronger test of the proposed transtheoretical relevance of reduced motivational incongruence.
The present findings have potential implications for motivational incongruence as a treatment target.
The motives assessed by the questionnaire refer to experiences and personenvironment transactions directly relevant to patients' everyday lives.

Their bottom-up origin and relatively concrete formulation may make them accessible to patients and therapists across different therapeutic backgrounds and facilitate their incorporation into individualized case formulations and treatment planning.
Motivational incongruence can be considered a potential treatment target at different levels of abstraction or specificity.

Depending on the questionnaire version and intended purpose, motivational incongruence may be assessed at the level of overall motivational incongruence, approach and avoidance incongruence, specific motivational dimensions, or individual motives.
At each level, reduced motivational incongruence could represent a candidate change mechanism.
In this study, we examined only total incongruence.
A next step would be to examine which dimensions of motivational incongruence predict subsequent psychological distress, for which patients, and under which circumstances.
Further research could then examine which therapeutic processes, including interventions, are associated with reductions in those dimensions.
Identifying such targets also requires considering that findings at the group level may not apply equally to individual patients (Huibers et al., 2021).

text.text: The present study has several strengths.

The prospective associations between motivational incongruence and psychological distress were examined across three psychotherapy samples, covering both controlled and routine-care treatment contexts.
Importantly, the statistical models separated stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations and estimated the prospective associations in both directions.
In addition, systematic change over treatment was accounted for in the main analyses and further addressed in the exploratory analyses.
Despite these strengths, several limitations should be considered.

First, while the analytic strategy strengthens the mechanism argument, the analyses do not establish causality, as timevarying factors associated with both motivational incongruence and psychological distress may still confound the observed prospective associations (Falkenström et al., 2020).
text.formatted: First, while the analytic strategy strengthens the mechanism argument, the analyses do not establish causality, as timevarying factors associated with both motivational incongruence and psychological distress may still confound the observed prospective associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Falkenström et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To more directly test causality, future research would need to identify interventions that reliably reduce motivational incongruence and examine their effects on motivational incongruence and subsequent outcomes in a controlled experimental setting (Kazdin, 2009).
text.formatted: To more directly test causality, future research would need to identify interventions that reliably reduce motivational incongruence and examine their effects on motivational incongruence and subsequent outcomes in a controlled experimental setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Kazdin, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the interpretation of cross-lagged associations depends on the time interval between assessments.
The actual lag through which motivational incongruence may influence psychological distress remains unknown, and the available assessment intervals differed across samples.

The present findings therefore establish prospective associations at the examined intervals but do not show that the same associations would be observed at shorter or longer intervals (Crits-Christoph & Gibbons, 2021; Falkenström, 2024).
text.formatted: The present findings therefore establish prospective associations at the examined intervals but do not show that the same associations would be observed at shorter or longer intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Crits-Christoph & Gibbons, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Falkenström, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The relevant lag may also vary between patients.
More intensive longitudinal assessments could help clarify the timescale of these associations.
Third, the analyses were based on manifest scale scores, meaning that measurement error was not modeled separately from the within-person fluctuations of interest.

Moreover, the more complex LCM-SRs yielded no admissible solutions in the Bern and Zurich samples, limiting our ability to examine the robustness of the findings when additionally accounting for individual time trends.

This limitation should be interpreted in light of recent methodological work cautioning that more extensive adjustment for stable or trend-like components in longitudinal panel models is not necessarily preferable in all settings.

Such adjustments can reduce some sources of bias, but may also introduce new bias when they absorb variance from dynamic processes, mediators, or posttreatment variation (Bailey et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025).

text.text: Fourth, both constructs were assessed by self-report only, and instruments differed across samples.
These measurement differences limit direct comparisons of effect sizes across samples.

Across three psychotherapy samples, prospective within-person associations between motivational incongruence and subsequent psychological distress support motivational incongruence as a potential change mechanism in psychotherapy.
The prospective relationship may also be partly reciprocal.
These findings suggest that motivational incongruence may represent a promising treatment target.
Future research is needed to test the proposed causal relationship experimentally and to examine which dimensions of motivational incongruence are most relevant for which patients.

text.text: After providing informed consent, patients were randomized to Exposure-Based Cognitive Therapy Revised (EBCT-R) or Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
Both conditions comprised up to 22 weekly sessions across three treatment phases.

The conditions differed most clearly during Phase 2: CBT targeted dysfunctional cognitions through cognitive restructuring and reality testing, whereas EBCT-R activated depressive networks and processed the activated material through emotion-focused techniques within an exposure framework.
Treatment was delivered by master's-level psychologists in postgraduate psychotherapy training (Grosse Holtforth et al., 2019).
